attributes.title: Level 3

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓Did you use [set sprite x] blocks to set the Player sprite’s acceleration y and velocity y?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the A button is pressed?

❓ What values should you input as the ay and vy parameters, so that the Player sprite is able to jump on top of platforms and fall down at a reasonable speed?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out different parameters in the [set sprite ay] and [set sprite vy] blocks. Remind them that in order for a sprite to jump up, a negative value must be used as the vy parameter.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by coding the Player sprite to jump on top of tilemap platforms!


In the [on button pressed] container already in the editor, add an [if then] conditional and replace the <true> value with an <is sprite hitting wall> block. Select the Player sprite’s name and [bottom] as the direction. Then, add a [set sprite [x]] block into the conditional and select [vy (velocity y)] from the drop-down.


Add another [set sprite [x]] block underneath the Player sprite’s blocks in the [on start] container. Use the drop-down to select [ay (acceleration y)].


Test out different values in the parameter of each block, so that the Player sprite is able to jump onto a platform and returns to the ground at a reasonable speed.


Click ▶ to explore the tilemap by making the Player sprite jump onto different platforms!

steps.hints: ❓Did you create the makeBee function with 2 parameters: number and Boolean?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What type of value will the (speed) parameter accept? 

❓ What type of value will the <isBeeDizzy> parameter accept? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that when the [makeBee] function is called, they will need to specify the values of each parameter. The (speed) parameter will require a numerical value, and the <isBeeDizzy> will require a Boolean.
steps.instructions:
Place moving Bee sprites on the tilemap for the Player sprite to collect!


Create a function called makeBee with two parameters: a number parameter named “speed” and a Boolean parameter named “isBeeDizzy”.


Drag the two Bee sprite blocks from the [on start] container into the [function makeBee] container. Then, set the Bee sprite’s velocity by adding a [set velocity to] block into the function container. Drag a (speed) bubble from the function container into both the vx and vy parameters.


Then, add a [set sprite bounce on wall] block into the function container.

steps.hints: ❓Did you replace the <true> value in the [if then] conditional with a <isBeeDizzy> Boolean from the function container?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Which animation makes the Bee sprite look “dizzy”?

❓ How is a function with two parameters different than one with only one parameter?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Remind the ninja to drag the <isBeeDizzy> Boolean from the function container into the [if then] conditional.

💡When a function is run, it runs the code in the function definition container, based on the parameters inputted in the [call function] block. When a function has multiple parameters, it has the ability to take in information for multiple data types.
steps.instructions:
Set some Bee sprites to be “dizzy” when they appear on the tilemap!


Add an [if then] conditional to the [function makeBee] container. Replace the <true> value with an <isBeeDizzy> Boolean from the function container.


Program the dizzy bee movement by adding an [animate movement] block inside the conditional. Select the Bee sprite name and a movement that makes the sprite look “dizzy”. Then, add an interval parameter and set the loop toggle to <ON>.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use a (pick random) block and a <% chance> value block in the [call makeBee] block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the [makeBee] function is called? 

❓ What do the values in the [call makeBee] block affect in the [function makeBee] container?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to connect the values inputted in the [call makeBee] block with the placement of the (speed) bubbles and <isBeeDizzy> Boolean in the function container, to understand how the parameters impact the Bee sprite’s appearance on screen.
steps.instructions:
The makeBee function wasn’t called, so no Bee sprites appeared on the tilemap!


Add a [call makeBee] block to the [on start] container and use Math blocks to add randomness to the Bee sprite’s speed and animation. 


Drag a (pick random) block into the (speed) parameter of the [call makeBee] block and use -50 and 50 as the values that the Bee sprite’s speed will randomly be selected between. 


Then, add a <% chance> value block into the <isBeeDizzy> parameter. Set the percentage to 30, so that 3 times out of 10, the Bee sprite will appear to be “dizzy”. 


Duplicate the entire [call makeBee] block and place it in the [on game update every ms] loop already in the editor.


Click ▶ to see Bee sprites appear on the tilemap every 5 seconds with varying speed and animations!

steps.hints: ❓Did you use a [while] loop to check for the length of the (array of sprites of kind (Bees))?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Did you select Bees as the sprite kind in (array of sprites of kind)?

❓ When does a [while] loop run? How long does it run for?

❓ Will there ever be more than 6 Bee sprites on the screen? Why or why not?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡A [while] loop will continue to run a chunk of code while a certain condition is true. In this example, the [while] loop will run while the number of Bee sprites on the screen is less than 6, and will stop running only when there are 6. 

💡 Because the [while] loop will only run while there are less than 6 Bee sprites on screen, there will never be more than 6 Bee sprites created. This is important because it represents the “stop” condition for the [while] loop, so that it doesn’t run infinitely.
steps.instructions:
Code the project to always have a total of 6 Bee sprites on the screen whenever the game is updated!


Open Loops and drag a [while] loop into the [on game update every ms] loop. Then, replace the <false> value with a <0 < 0> comparison block. Make sure less than (<) is selected from the dropdown and type “6” into the right parameter.


Drag a (length of array) bubble into the left parameter of the comparison block and replace the (list) value with (array of sprites of kind (Bees)).


Then, move the [call makeBee] block inside the [while] loop, so that the [makeBee] function is called while there are less than 6 Bee sprites on the screen.


Click ▶ to see Bee sprites reappear on the screen when there are less than 6 left!

steps.hints: ❓Did you use an [if then] conditional to check the length of the (array of sprites of kind (Bees))?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Under what condition will the game end in a win?

❓ How many seconds does the Player sprite have to collect all 6 Bee sprites? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Prompt the ninja to identify the parameter in the [on game update every ms] loop (5000 ms or 5 seconds) to notice how long the Player sprite has to collect all 6 Bee sprites.
steps.instructions:
End the game in a win when the Player sprite collects all of the on-screen Bee sprites!


Add an [if then] conditional to the [forever] loop already in the editor. Then, duplicate the comparison block from the [while] loop and place it in the <true> space. Change the symbol in the drop down to equal to (=) and type “0” in the right parameter.


Then, place a [game over] block inside the conditional and set the toggle to <WIN>.


Click ▶ to see if the Player sprite can catch all of the Bee sprites before they reappear on the screen!

steps.hints: ❓Did you add customizations to your project, such as dialog boxes, splash screens, or effects?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What directions might help a user understand how to play the game?

❓ What other effects might be added to make the game more exciting to play?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Guide ninjas to note that while these customizing blocks are open ended and not required for the game to “work”, they really improve the Player’s experience playing a game, either by giving context to what the Player should do or not do, or to provide a more fun experience overall. They also allow the Ninja to add their personal touch and express themselves through small details present in the game.
steps.instructions:
Make the project more engaging by adding directions with a dialog box and frame, setting a background color, and including any sound or visual effects.


Click ▶ to see the completed project!

subgroups.introduction: Create a project that uses a while loop to add new Enemy sprites while a specific condition is true.

validationItems.text: Player sprite jumps up when the A button is pressed and the bottom of the sprite is touching a tilemap wall tile.
Bee sprite is created by a function with 2 parameters; one that controls velocity (speed) and one that controls animation (isBeeDizzy).
Bee sprite function is called with both parameters.
Bee sprites appear on game update so that there are 6 total Bee sprites on screen.
End the game when the Player sprite collects all the on-screen Bee sprites.
Game instructions are shared in a dialog box. Sound and visual effects are added to the game.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 3 of Green Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about [for index] and [while] loops. These loops can be used to control the placement of sprites on a tilemap and make something happen while a certain condition is true. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 3:

badges.title: Around and Around
badges.description: Use advanced loops that offer more control options to repeat code in a project.

badges.title: Card Catalog
badges.description: Use a loop that counts from 0 to a given number to repeat a section of code.

badges.title: Waiting for Things to Change
badges.description: Use a loop that will repeat a section of code while a condition is true.
